headline: Mammals are warm-blooded, milk-producing, hair-covered animals—including us
universal_truth: Recognizing what we share with others creates empathy; seeing ourselves in them changes our relationship
fun_facts: All mammals—from bats to whales—share common features: milk, hair, and warm blood
The blue whale is the largest mammal—and the largest animal ever to exist
There are only about 6,400 mammal species, compared to over a million insect species
discussion_questions: What makes mammals seem more 'like us' than other animals?
Why might we feel more empathy for mammals than for fish or insects?
What traits do all mammals share?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: We're mammals—part of a group that includes elephants and mice, whales and bats, dogs and dolphins. What unites us? Warm blood, hair, and the defining feature: mothers produce milk. We're all members of the same club.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Mammals seem incredibly diverse—flying bats, swimming whales, underground moles. What could a human possibly share with a mouse or a whale? What makes us all mammals?
cliff.prompt: What do all mammals have in common?

options.text: Warm blood, hair or fur, and females that produce milk to feed their young
options.response: Yes. These three features define mammals. Every mammal, regardless of size or habitat, shares this basic biology. We're more alike than we appear.

options.text: Live birth and parental care distinguish mammals from other animals
options.response: Most mammals give live birth, but platypuses lay eggs. Milk production is the true defining feature...

q1.title: Milk Makers
q1.script: The word 'mammal' comes from 'mammary'—milk glands. All mammal mothers produce milk. This allows extended care of young, time for brains to develop, and strong parent-child bonds. Milk is what makes us mammals.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Milk Makers"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Warm Inside
q2.script: Mammals maintain constant body temperature regardless of environment—we're warm-blooded. This requires lots of food but allows activity in any climate. A mammal works in Arctic cold or desert heat because it regulates itself.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Minority Group
q3.script: There are only about 6,400 mammal species—tiny compared to a million insects or 30,000 fish. We're a small, specialized group. But mammals dominate many ecosystems and include the largest animals that ever lived.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Recognizing what we share creates empathy. Other mammals nurse their young, feel pain, form bonds. Seeing ourselves in them changes our relationship—from dominion to kinship.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 140. Tomorrow, we'll explore cold-blooded survivors—reptiles. Until then, look at another mammal and recognize a relative: warm blood, hair, milk. We're family.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Mammal Kinship - Recognize Family
growTrack.activity: Observe a mammal today—a pet, a squirrel, any mammal. Remember: their mothers made milk, they have hair, they regulate their temperature. You share these fundamental traits. How does recognizing kinship change how you see them?
